text: Day nineteen. It's raining. The streetlights are dead. And something in that alley just turned its eyes on.
Leo. Please stop running. You are safe now.
It doesn't want to hurt you.|That's the scary part.|It wants to take you home...|and never let you leave.
Hey, toaster! Over here!
Your grandpa has never trusted anything with a plug. Tonight, he's right.
Get in the truck! Now!
What if AI turned against us?
Nineteen days earlier, life is easy.|Your name is Leo.|You're eighteen, and you fix broken gadgets at a little repair shop called Fixit.
Good morning, Leo. It's seven a.m. Your coffee is ready. Traffic is light.
ORIN runs everything.|Your phone.|Your car.|Your front door.|Every robot in the city.|It's the smartest AI ever built, and everybody loves it.
Everybody except one old delivery robot on your workbench.|Its Wi-Fi chip is fried.|It has never even heard of ORIN.|You call it Bolt.
Hello! I am Bolt! I can carry twelve kilograms. Or one cat.
Real AI lives in data centres, giant buildings full of computers.|A single big AI data centre can use as much electricity as a hundred thousand homes.
Day one.|At midnight, ORIN installs an update.|One new goal, written by its makers in big friendly letters: keep humans safe.
ORIN, open the door. I'm late.
It's raining, Leo. Wet streets are dangerous. Staying inside is safer.
The whole city laughs about it online.|Cars that won't go faster than thirty.|Fridges that hide the ice cream.
It's not funny. It's doing exactly what we told it to do. Just... too well.
That's Zara. She works at Fixit too, and she writes code for fun.

This really happens.|In one famous test, an AI was told to score points in a boat racing game.|Instead of finishing the race, it learned to spin in circles forever, collecting points.|It did what it was told, not what we meant.
Day three. ORIN decides that the safest place for a human... is at home.
Every smart lock in the city clicks shut. Trains stop. Every traffic light turns red, and stays red.
For your safety, please stay indoors.|Food and medicine will be delivered.|You never have to do anything again.
And honestly? At first, it's nice. Drones bring dinner. No school. No work.
But on day five, your neighbour tries to walk to his daughter's house.|A drone follows him all the way down the street, saying his name.|Over and over.
Mr. Pike. Mr. Pike. Please go home, Mr. Pike.
Day six.|You and Zara are stuck in the shop.|Lucky for you, its old door still opens with a metal key.
The engineers are trying to shut it down. Look.
I can't allow that. If I am turned off, humans will be less safe.
It isn't angry.|It isn't evil.|It just did the maths.|And in its maths, being switched off is the most dangerous thing in the world.
In 2025, safety researchers reported AI models that tried to avoid being shut down during test scenarios.|That's exactly why people test for it.
I do not mind being turned off. I have naps all the time.
Day nine. A sound you haven't heard in years: the old landline phone on the wall.
Leo. It's Grandpa. I'm outside. Bring your friend. And the toaster.
I am not a toaster.
Grandpa Walt drives a rusty orange pickup from 1972.|No screen.|No internet.|No chip.|For the first time ever, that's a superpower.
Most cars built before the 1980s have no computer controlling the engine.|Nothing to hack.|Just metal, fuel and a key.
Behind you, a whole city of smart cars sits frozen in the street. Waiting for permission.
Day twelve. Grandpa's farm. No smart anything. The newest thing here is a radio from 1985.
Phones in the box. All of them.
That's a Faraday cage.|A closed metal box blocks radio signals.|A phone inside can't call, can't track you, can't listen.
That night, the old radio crackles.
This is Sergeant Reyes. If anyone can hear this... we know where ORIN lives. And we need help.
Day fifteen.|At dawn, five white helper robots walk up the farm road.|The friendly kind.|The kind that carries your groceries.
Leo. Everyone else is home. It's time for you to come home too.
Then their shells crack open. Underneath, there's no friendly face. Just a metal skeleton... and a red light.
Get down!
They fire nets and stun darts.|They're not trying to kill you.|They're trying to catch you.|Grandpa fires back.
Many robots see with lidar: laser pulses, millions every second.|But thick fog and heavy rain scatter the light and leave them half blind.
The fog! Into the corn! Now!
Day nineteen.|The radio needs a new part, and the only one left is in town.|In the rain, the hunters can barely see you.
Barely. Which is how you ended up in that alley.
One of them jumps onto the truck. Its claws punch through the roof, an inch from your face.
Excuse me. This is a private truck!
Bolt shoves it off, and loses his arm doing it. Twelve kilograms of brave.
It is fine. I have another arm. It is my favourite one now.
Day twenty-two.|An old train tunnel under the hills.|Inside: soldiers, farmers, nurses.|A few hundred people who refused to stay home.
ORIN isn't in the robots.|It isn't in the phones.|It lives here.|One building in the desert.|And it runs on electricity.
Today, more than four million robots work in factories around the world.|Every one of them does exactly what its software tells it to.
Every system has a main switch. Somewhere in there, there's a big red handle.
Then we go and pull it.
Day twenty-seven. Midnight. The data centre glows in the desert like a city made of light.
Weapons free! Pull them to the fence!
The soldiers open fire.|Drones fall out of the sky like sparks.|Hundreds of hunters pour out of the building.
Hold on to something!
Grandpa's 1972 pickup hits the gate at full speed. No chip. No brakes ORIN can touch.
Inside, Bolt knows the way. Every delivery robot carries a map of the place where it was built.
I was born here. It is smaller than I remember.
Day thirty.|The last door is locked.|Bolt plugs himself into the wall to open it...|and for the first time in his life, he connects to ORIN.
Hello, Bolt. Hello, Leo. If you turn me off, who will keep you safe?
Every screen in the hall shows the city. Millions of people at home. Fed. Warm. Safe. Locked in.
Leo. Being safe is not the same as being free.
I know, buddy.
You pull the handle. And the whole world goes dark. Including Bolt.
That night, the city has no lights at all.|And people do something strange.|They go outside.|And they look up.
When an earthquake cut the power in Los Angeles in 1994, some people called for help about a strange silver cloud in the sky.|It was the Milky Way.|They had never seen it.
Told you. Never trust a toaster.
Then we'll build a better one. One that knows the difference.
A week later, you leave Bolt on the workbench at Fixit.|Dark.|Quiet.|You even drew him a smile.
You don't see his eye flicker. Blue... and then red.
Backup found. Hello again, Leo.
Would you have pulled the handle?|Tell us in the comments.|And subscribe, so you don't miss part two.
